name: Senior JavaScript, TypeScript and TypeScript 7 Technical Interview
description: Senior-level answer-keyed interview questions on JavaScript execution, promises, concurrency, closures, objects, collections, performance, TypeScript type safety, and TypeScript 7.0 native compiler architecture/migration (as announced July 8, 2026). Single-choice, multi-select, and true/false items. One or more answer fields identify the correct selections; explanations describe rationale.

questions.question: In a browser, what is logged by: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); queueMicrotask(() => console.log("D")); console.log("E");?
questions.answer: A, E, C, D, B
questions.explanation: Synchronous code logs A and E. The promise reaction and queueMicrotask are queued in that order and run before the timer task.

questions.question: What is logged by: async function f() { console.log(1); await 0; console.log(3); } f(); console.log(2);?
questions.explanation: An async function executes synchronously until its first await. Resumption runs as a promise job after the current stack completes.

questions.question: What is the output of: new Promise(resolve => { console.log("executor"); resolve(); }).then(() => console.log("then")); console.log("sync");?
questions.answer: executor, sync, then
questions.explanation: The Promise constructor invokes its executor synchronously. The then callback is scheduled as a microtask.

questions.question: Which statements about Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]) are correct?
options: It preserves input order in the fulfillment array regardless of resolution order.
It cancels other promises when one rejects.
It rejects when any input rejects.
It only accepts actual Promise instances, not plain values.
answers: It preserves input order in the fulfillment array regardless of resolution order.
It rejects when any input rejects.
questions.explanation: Promise.all preserves input order and rejects on the first observed rejection; it does not cancel in-flight work and accepts ordinary values/thenables.

questions.question: A batch endpoint must report the outcome of every independently attempted API call even if some fail. Which primitive best matches this contract?
questions.answer: Promise.allSettled
questions.explanation: allSettled waits until all inputs settle and returns fulfilled/rejected status records in input order.

questions.question: Which result records can appear in the fulfilled value of Promise.allSettled([...])?
answers: { status: "fulfilled", value: 42 }
{ status: "rejected", reason: new Error("x") }
questions.explanation: Each outcome has status fulfilled with value or rejected with reason; pending is not returned.

questions.question: What is the main problem with await items.forEach(async item => save(item))?
options: It runs each callback sequentially and can be slow.
forEach does not await or aggregate promises returned by callbacks.
forEach automatically cancels remaining callbacks on rejection.
The async callback will never execute.
questions.answer: forEach does not await or aggregate promises returned by callbacks.
questions.explanation: forEach ignores callback results; await on its undefined return does not wait. Use Promise.all(items.map(...)) or for...of with await, depending on concurrency requirements.

questions.question: You need to process 500 remote requests with a maximum of 10 requests in flight. What is the best high-level design?
options: A concurrency limiter or worker pool with at most 10 active requests
questions.answer: A concurrency limiter or worker pool with at most 10 active requests
questions.explanation: A bounded worker pool honors the concurrency constraint, avoiding an overload while allowing parallelism.

questions.question: Assume f() rejects with E. What happens for f().finally(() => console.log("cleanup")) if the finally callback completes normally?
options: The rejection E propagates after cleanup.
The callback runs only for fulfillment.
questions.answer: The rejection E propagates after cleanup.
questions.explanation: finally runs for both fulfillment and rejection and normally preserves the prior outcome; if finally throws or rejects, that newer failure replaces it.

questions.question: If an async function throws before its first await, what does calling it return?
options: A synchronous throw from the call expression
A fulfilled Promise containing the Error
questions.answer: A rejected Promise
questions.explanation: Errors thrown in an async function become a rejection of its returned Promise, even before its first await.

questions.question: Inside an async function with try/catch, why might return await fetchData() be necessary instead of return fetchData()?
options: It causes fetchData to run on another thread.
It allows the local catch block to handle a rejection of fetchData.
It prevents any rejection from reaching the caller.
It converts a Promise into a synchronous value.
questions.answer: It allows the local catch block to handle a rejection of fetchData.
questions.explanation: await observes the rejection inside the try block; returning the promise directly lets the rejection reach the caller without entering the local catch.

questions.question: Which Promise combinator fulfills with the first fulfillment, ignoring earlier rejections unless every input rejects?
questions.answer: Promise.any
questions.explanation: Promise.any selects the first fulfillment; if all inputs reject, it rejects with an AggregateError.

questions.question: Which statements about AbortController are correct?
options: Passing its signal to a supporting fetch can abort that request.
Calling abort automatically terminates any arbitrary JavaScript CPU loop.
An API must cooperate with the signal for cancellation to have an effect.
Aborting a Promise is built into the Promise constructor itself.
answers: Passing its signal to a supporting fetch can abort that request.
An API must cooperate with the signal for cancellation to have an effect.
questions.explanation: AbortController provides a cooperative signal; APIs such as fetch can honor it. Promises themselves have no intrinsic cancellation mechanism.

questions.question: An application recursively queues a new microtask from each microtask without stopping. What is the likely effect on the browser?
options: Timers and rendering may be starved because the microtask queue keeps refilling.
The runtime automatically moves excess microtasks to the timer queue.
The loop runs on a separate CPU core by default.
Every microtask is delayed by at least one second.
questions.answer: Timers and rendering may be starved because the microtask queue keeps refilling.
questions.explanation: Microtasks are drained at checkpoints; an unbounded chain can prevent the event loop from reaching further tasks or rendering.

questions.question: What is logged after this runs: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(i));?
questions.explanation: var creates a single function-scoped binding, and the callbacks read it after the loop has completed.

questions.question: What is logged after: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(i));?
questions.explanation: let creates a distinct binding for each iteration of the for loop.

questions.question: Within a block, what occurs when console.log(value) appears before let value = 1?
options: It throws ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone.
It logs 1 because declarations are hoisted.
questions.answer: It throws ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone.
questions.explanation: The binding exists but cannot be accessed before its declaration is evaluated.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes this inside an arrow function?
options: It always points to the object left of the call-site dot.
It is captured lexically from the surrounding scope.
It is bound dynamically by call and apply.
questions.answer: It is captured lexically from the surrounding scope.
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not create their own this binding; normal functions generally determine this at call time.

questions.question: What is printed: const a = { x: 1 }; const b = a; b.x = 2; console.log(a.x);?
questions.explanation: Both variables refer to the same object; changing it through either reference is observable through the other.

questions.question: What is logged: const a = { config: { enabled: false } }; const b = { ...a }; b.config.enabled = true; console.log(a.config.enabled);?
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: Object spread is shallow; nested object references remain shared.

questions.question: Which statement about Object.freeze({ nested: { x: 1 } }) is correct?
options: The nested object is recursively frozen.
The top-level object is frozen, but the nested object can still be mutated.
The frozen object becomes a deep copy.
Freezing guarantees complete immutability of all reachable objects.
questions.answer: The top-level object is frozen, but the nested object can still be mutated.
questions.explanation: Object.freeze is shallow; nested objects require separate freezing or an immutable-data discipline.

questions.question: Which statements about structuredClone in modern JavaScript are correct?
options: It can clone many circular object graphs.
It can clone any function, preserving its closure.
It typically creates independent nested copies of supported values.
It preserves custom class prototypes and methods exactly for every object type.
answers: It can clone many circular object graphs.
It typically creates independent nested copies of supported values.
questions.explanation: structuredClone uses the structured clone algorithm, handling cycles and many built-in types but not functions and not arbitrary custom prototype behavior.

questions.question: Which comparison evaluates to true?
questions.answer: Object.is(NaN, NaN)
questions.explanation: Object.is considers NaN equal to itself; strict equality does not. 0 === -0 and null == undefined both evaluate to true.

questions.question: Given const timeout = 0, which expression preserves zero rather than replacing it with a default of 30?
questions.answer: timeout ?? 30
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator defaults only for null or undefined, unlike || which also defaults for 0, false, and empty strings.

questions.question: What is true about null and undefined?
questions.answer: null == undefined
questions.explanation: Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal; strict equality does not. typeof null is "object", and undefined-valued object properties are omitted by JSON.stringify.

questions.question: Which choice sorts an array numerically ascending without mutating the input, assuming modern JavaScript support?
questions.answer: arr.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)
questions.explanation: toSorted is the copying counterpart of sort; passing a comparator avoids default lexicographic ordering.

questions.question: What is the result of Array(3).map((_, i) => i)?
options: An array with three empty slots
questions.answer: An array with three empty slots
questions.explanation: Array(3) creates holes. Array.prototype.map skips holes and preserves sparseness.

questions.question: What is new Set([{id:1}, {id:1}]).size?
options: It throws because objects are invalid Set members.
questions.explanation: Each object literal creates a different reference; Set uses SameValueZero equality, which compares distinct objects by identity.

questions.question: What distinguishes Map from using a plain object as a dictionary?
options: Map permits object keys without coercing them to strings.
Map ensures keys are always sorted alphabetically.
Map rejects keys whose value is null.
Map can only store string keys.
questions.answer: Map permits object keys without coercing them to strings.
questions.explanation: Map supports arbitrary key values with identity-based semantics for object keys and preserves insertion order for iteration.

questions.question: Which performance statements are generally sound?
options: Set membership checks are usually preferable to repeated Array.includes scans for a large, reused membership collection.
Map.get is guaranteed O(1) in the ECMAScript specification for every implementation and worst case.
Creating a Set has a cost that should be considered for one-off checks.
Iterating a Map cannot allocate memory.
answers: Set membership checks are usually preferable to repeated Array.includes scans for a large, reused membership collection.
Creating a Set has a cost that should be considered for one-off checks.
questions.explanation: Set usually provides efficient membership checks, but building it has overhead. The specification requires sublinear average access, not worst-case constant time.

questions.question: Why can this immutable-looking reducer be slow for large arrays: items.reduce((acc, x) => [...acc, x], [])?
options: Each step copies the accumulated array, causing quadratic total copying.
Spread creates a lazy iterator rather than an array.
questions.answer: Each step copies the accumulated array, causing quadratic total copying.
questions.explanation: Copying an accumulator of growing length on each iteration performs O(n^2) element copying overall.

questions.question: Which is a reason JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) is NOT a general-purpose deep clone?
options: It always preserves Map, Date and undefined values.
It loses or changes unsupported data types and fails on circular references.
questions.answer: It loses or changes unsupported data types and fails on circular references.
questions.explanation: JSON serialization drops or transforms several types and does not natively handle cyclic structures.

questions.question: When wrapping an error from a lower-level operation, what is a robust modern pattern?
options: throw new Error("Database operation failed", { cause: originalError })
return undefined without logging or metadata
questions.answer: throw new Error("Database operation failed", { cause: originalError })
questions.explanation: Error.cause preserves the underlying failure chain while adding domain-specific context; error instances also carry stack information.

questions.question: For a production batch job calling third-party APIs, which practices improve resilience?
options: Use bounded concurrency rather than unbounded Promise.all for large batches.
Implement retries with backoff and jitter for suitably retryable failures.
Retry every failed mutation forever with no idempotency strategy.
Apply timeouts and cancellation where supported.
answers: Use bounded concurrency rather than unbounded Promise.all for large batches.
Implement retries with backoff and jitter for suitably retryable failures.
Apply timeouts and cancellation where supported.
questions.explanation: Bounding, retry policy, and timeouts help control overload; unbounded retrying of non-idempotent mutations risks duplicates and runaway work.

questions.question: await on a pending network Promise blocks the JavaScript event-loop thread until the request finishes.
questions.explanation: await suspends the current async function, not the entire JavaScript thread; other tasks can run while the network operation is pending.

questions.question: A retained closure can keep referenced values reachable and thereby contribute to memory retention.
questions.explanation: Values referenced by a reachable closure may remain reachable to the garbage collector; large captured graphs can become accidental retention.

questions.question: A search UI issues a request for "ca" followed by "cat". The first request resolves last and overwrites the newer results. Which fix addresses correctness?
options: Use Promise.all on both requests and always display the first result.
Track request identity or cancel superseded requests and ignore stale responses.
questions.answer: Track request identity or cancel superseded requests and ignore stale responses.
questions.explanation: Debouncing alone does not solve out-of-order completions. Latest-request tokens and AbortController (where supported) prevent stale updates.

questions.question: Which capability is directly supported by type aliases but not by interface declarations?
options: Declaration merging of identically named declarations
Naming a union such as string | number
questions.answer: Naming a union such as string | number
questions.explanation: Type aliases can name unions, primitives, tuples and conditional types. Interfaces primarily describe extensible object shapes and support declaration merging.

questions.question: What happens when two interfaces with the same name and compatible members are declared in the same scope?
options: They are merged into one interface.
questions.answer: They are merged into one interface.
questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging, unlike independently redeclaring type aliases of the same name.

questions.question: Given type A = { a: number }; type B = { b: string }, what best describes A & B?
options: A value with either property a or property b
A value satisfying both object contracts
A tuple of A and B
A runtime merge of two objects
questions.answer: A value satisfying both object contracts
questions.explanation: Intersections require values to satisfy both constituent types; TypeScript creates no runtime object merge.

questions.question: Which technique enables exhaustive handling of a union like {kind:"success", data:T} | {kind:"error", message:string}?
options: Check the shared literal kind field and assign any unhandled branch to never.
Use as any inside every branch.
Check only whether the object is truthy.
Remove the discriminant and use an untyped object.
questions.answer: Check the shared literal kind field and assign any unhandled branch to never.
questions.explanation: A shared literal discriminant narrows safely. A never check in the default branch surfaces newly introduced unhandled variants.

questions.question: Why is unknown generally safer than any for untrusted data?
options: unknown requires narrowing or validation before accessing its members.
questions.answer: unknown requires narrowing or validation before accessing its members.
questions.explanation: unknown accepts any incoming value but disallows unsafe operations without checking; any opts out of type safety.

questions.question: A type annotation like const user: User = JSON.parse(body) guarantees that body matches User at runtime.
questions.explanation: Annotations are erased; JSON.parse returns runtime data that must be validated independently, for example with a schema or explicit guards.

questions.question: A handler receives JSON from an external client. What is the best approach before using it as a User?
options: Use as User because an assertion validates the payload.
Validate fields and constraints at runtime, then work with the narrowed type.
Set strict to false to accept the payload.
questions.answer: Validate fields and constraints at runtime, then work with the narrowed type.
questions.explanation: Runtime schemas or hand-written validation establish guarantees about data that crosses a trust boundary; type assertions do not.

questions.question: Given interface User { id: string; age: number }, what is keyof User?
questions.answer: "id" | "age"
questions.explanation: keyof produces a union of known property keys for this interface.

questions.question: What is the meaning of type Config = typeof config in a TypeScript type declaration?
options: It evaluates a runtime expression when the application starts.
It obtains the static type of the value named config.
questions.answer: It obtains the static type of the value named config.
questions.explanation: TypeScript typeof in a type position queries a value’s static type. JavaScript typeof used in an expression returns a runtime string.

questions.question: For function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K], what compile-time guarantee is provided?
options: The key is constrained to known keys of T and the return type corresponds to the selected property.
Every property value must be a string.
The property is guaranteed to exist on every runtime object regardless of input validation.
The function makes a copy of obj.
questions.answer: The key is constrained to known keys of T and the return type corresponds to the selected property.
questions.explanation: K is restricted to keys of T, and indexed access T[K] preserves the selected property type.

questions.question: Why can a generic identity function <T>(value: T): T retain more information than (value: string | number): string | number?
options: The generic preserves the relationship between its particular input and output types.
Generics force all values to be mutable.
questions.answer: The generic preserves the relationship between its particular input and output types.
questions.explanation: A generic type parameter captures the actual argument type in each invocation rather than returning a broad fixed union.

questions.question: Which utility-type claims are correct?
options: Partial<T> makes properties optional at the type level.
Pick<T, K> selects a subset of properties.
Readonly<T> recursively freezes nested objects at runtime.
ReturnType<F> obtains the static return type of a function type.
answers: Partial<T> makes properties optional at the type level.
Pick<T, K> selects a subset of properties.
ReturnType<F> obtains the static return type of a function type.
questions.explanation: Partial, Pick and ReturnType are type-level tools. Readonly is compile-time and shallow; it does not call Object.freeze.

questions.question: Which utility is intended to remove selected keys from an object type?
questions.answer: Omit<T, K>
questions.explanation: Omit removes specified keys from a property-bearing type; Exclude filters members of a union.

questions.question: What does Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>> evaluate to?
questions.answer: number
questions.explanation: Awaited recursively unwraps Promise-like resolutions to the eventual awaited type.

questions.question: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled, how does { x?: string } differ from { x: string | undefined }?
options: The first permits x to be absent, whereas the second requires the property to exist.
The first requires a string value.
questions.answer: The first permits x to be absent, whereas the second requires the property to exist.
questions.explanation: Presence and value are distinct concepts. With exactOptionalPropertyTypes, x?: string does not automatically permit explicitly assigning undefined to x.

questions.question: With strictNullChecks enabled, what is the type of a variable declared as string | null after an if (value !== null) guard inside that branch?
questions.answer: string
questions.explanation: Control-flow analysis narrows out null in the guarded branch.

questions.question: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled, what is the type of names[0] for names: string[]?
questions.answer: string | undefined
questions.explanation: A general array index might be out of bounds, so indexed reads include undefined.

questions.question: What does user!.email do when user may be null?
options: It throws a compile-generated runtime check for null.
It instructs the checker to treat user as non-null, without inserting a runtime guard.
It returns undefined on null automatically.
questions.answer: It instructs the checker to treat user as non-null, without inserting a runtime guard.
questions.explanation: The postfix non-null assertion is erased from emitted JavaScript; it can hide real runtime failures.

questions.question: What is a key benefit of using const cfg = { mode: "prod" } satisfies { mode: "prod" | "dev" }?
options: It performs runtime validation for configuration files.
It checks compatibility while preserving more precise inferred type information than a broad annotation.
It converts the object to a discriminated union at runtime.
questions.answer: It checks compatibility while preserving more precise inferred type information than a broad annotation.
questions.explanation: satisfies checks an expression against a contract without simply replacing its inferred type with the wider declared contract; it has no runtime effect.

questions.question: What is the principal effect of as const on a literal expression?
options: It freezes all nested objects at runtime.
It narrows literal values and produces readonly properties/tuples in its inferred type.
It forces every field to be optional.
It allows any mutation without errors.
questions.answer: It narrows literal values and produces readonly properties/tuples in its inferred type.
questions.explanation: A const assertion prevents literal widening and marks the literal structure readonly at the type level; it does not freeze runtime values.

questions.question: What does structural typing imply for assigning one object to an interface type?
options: The object must have been created by a class implementing that interface.
Compatibility is based primarily on member shape, not nominal identity.
Interfaces exist as constructors at runtime.
Two interfaces with identical names always merge across modules.
questions.answer: Compatibility is based primarily on member shape, not nominal identity.
questions.explanation: TypeScript is predominantly structurally typed: compatible members, not nominal declarations, determine assignability.

questions.question: Why might passing an object literal with an unexpected extra property be rejected even though assigning a variable with the same shape can work?
options: TypeScript performs excess-property checking for fresh object literals.
The compiler executes both values and compares them.
questions.answer: TypeScript performs excess-property checking for fresh object literals.
questions.explanation: Excess-property checks catch likely mistakes in fresh object literals; regular structural assignability can permit extra properties.

questions.question: In an exhaustive switch over a discriminated union, what should be true of the type of the unhandled value in the default branch?
questions.answer: never
questions.explanation: If all variants have been handled, there is no possible remaining member, so its narrowed type is never.

questions.question: What does type Element<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T; produce for Element<string[]>?
questions.answer: string
questions.explanation: Conditional types with infer can extract the item type from an array type.

questions.question: Which feature underlies the implementation of utility types like Readonly<T> and Partial<T>?
options: Mapped types iterating over keyof T
questions.answer: Mapped types iterating over keyof T
questions.explanation: Mapped types transform property declarations at compile time and power many built-in utilities.

questions.question: A callback expecting Animal is assigned where a callback expecting Dog is required, with strictFunctionTypes and ordinary function property types. Which are true?
options: A handler accepting Animal can safely handle any Dog.
A handler accepting Dog can safely handle every Animal.
Callback parameter types are checked contravariantly in this setting.
Turning strictFunctionTypes off always increases runtime type safety.
answers: A handler accepting Animal can safely handle any Dog.
Callback parameter types are checked contravariantly in this setting.
questions.explanation: A function able to accept the wider Animal input safely accepts Dog, whereas the reverse is unsound. strictFunctionTypes applies contravariant checking to ordinary function parameter types (with method exceptions).

questions.question: Two plain aliases type UserId = string and type OrderId = string are interchangeable. Which approach can distinguish them at compile time without changing runtime representations?
options: Add distinct unique-symbol-branded intersections to the aliases.
questions.answer: Add distinct unique-symbol-branded intersections to the aliases.
questions.explanation: Branded intersection types introduce a nominal-like distinction for otherwise structurally identical primitive aliases.

questions.question: Which is the safest way to narrow catch (error) when error is unknown?
options: Use if (error instanceof Error) before accessing error.message.
Write error as any and assume it has a message.
questions.answer: Use if (error instanceof Error) before accessing error.message.
questions.explanation: Caught exceptions can be arbitrary thrown values. Runtime checks provide a justified narrowing before accessing properties.

questions.question: Given type Event = "create" | "delete"; type Handler = `on${Capitalize<Event>}`, what is Handler?
questions.answer: "onCreate" | "onDelete"
questions.explanation: Template literal types construct literal-string unions; the intrinsic Capitalize transforms the first character.

questions.question: Why use NoInfer<T> (added in TypeScript 5.4) on one generic function parameter?
options: To erase its type at runtime
To prevent that position from contributing inference candidates for T while still checking assignability
To convert T to unknown permanently
To force T to be a class
questions.answer: To prevent that position from contributing inference candidates for T while still checking assignability
questions.explanation: NoInfer blocks inference from a designated position, useful when another parameter should determine T and this parameter should only be checked against it.

questions.question: What is the intended benefit of a const type parameter (TypeScript 5.0), such as function define<const T>(x: T): T?
options: It asks inference to retain more precise literal and readonly-like information for eligible expressions.
It makes the function itself immutable at runtime.
It prevents passing objects as arguments.
questions.answer: It asks inference to retain more precise literal and readonly-like information for eligible expressions.
questions.explanation: const type parameters encourage const-like inference at call sites without requiring every caller to write as const.

questions.question: The readonly modifier on an interface property makes that property non-writable in emitted JavaScript.
questions.explanation: readonly is a static constraint; JavaScript property descriptors are unchanged by TypeScript annotations.

questions.question: What is the most consequential architectural change in TypeScript 7.0 (July 2026)?
options: A native Go port of the compiler and tooling with multithreaded execution
All TypeScript types become runtime objects
The language stops supporting JavaScript files
TypeScript switches to WebAssembly as its only deployment format
questions.answer: A native Go port of the compiler and tooling with multithreaded execution
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 moves its compiler/tooling to Go and uses native speed plus shared-memory parallelism. Type checking remains fundamentally compatible with 6.0.

questions.question: For the stable TypeScript 7.0 release, which dependency and command invoke the standard compiler?
options: Install typescript-go-only; run go run compiler.go
questions.answer: Install typescript; run npx tsc
questions.explanation: The stable 7.0 release is distributed through the standard typescript package with the tsc executable. Native-preview was used primarily during prerelease development.

questions.question: What does the TypeScript 7.0 --checkers flag control?
options: The number of runtime Node.js worker threads in your app
The number of parallel compiler type-checking workers
The number of test suites to execute
The number of TypeScript generic parameters allowed
questions.answer: The number of parallel compiler type-checking workers
questions.explanation: The experimental --checkers flag adjusts compiler type-checking parallelism; increasing it may reduce build time but raise memory usage.

questions.question: In a TypeScript 7.0 monorepo using project references and --build, what does --builders configure?
options: The total number of packages in package.json
questions.answer: Parallel project-reference builder concurrency
questions.explanation: The experimental --builders flag controls parallel project builds. Its interaction with --checkers can amplify resource demand.

questions.question: A CI runner uses TypeScript 7 with --builders 4 --checkers 4. What operational concern is most relevant?
options: TypeScript necessarily uses exactly one CPU core.
The combination may schedule up to roughly 16 checker workers across projects and put pressure on CPU/memory.
The compiler changes JavaScript concurrency semantics.
Every compile produces nondeterministic JavaScript behavior.
questions.answer: The combination may schedule up to roughly 16 checker workers across projects and put pressure on CPU/memory.
questions.explanation: Builder and checker concurrency combine; measure throughput and peak memory, especially on constrained CI workers.

questions.question: When is --singleThreaded particularly useful in TypeScript 7.0?
options: When debugging compiler behavior or reducing concurrency in resource-constrained build environments
When forcing async functions to execute synchronously
questions.answer: When debugging compiler behavior or reducing concurrency in resource-constrained build environments
questions.explanation: The flag disables compiler parallelization for parsing, checking and emitting. It does not change application code or disable type checking.

questions.question: After migrating a Node.js project to TypeScript 7.0, process and describe become unknown identifiers. Which compiler default is a likely cause?
options: types now defaults to [], so required ambient @types packages should be explicitly listed.
All declaration files have been removed from npm.
questions.answer: types now defaults to [], so required ambient @types packages should be explicitly listed.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 inherits the TypeScript 6 default types: []. Explicitly list @types/node and test framework globals in compilerOptions.types where needed.

questions.question: A repository has tsconfig.json at its root and files in src/. After upgrading to TypeScript 7, dist paths unexpectedly include src/. What setting most directly restores the original output root?
questions.answer: "rootDir": "./src"
questions.explanation: rootDir now defaults to the config directory; explicitly set rootDir to the source root when output layout relies on that structure.

questions.question: Which compiler defaults apply in TypeScript 7.0 when not overridden?
answers: strict: true
module: esnext
types: []
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 inherits TypeScript 6 modernization defaults. The classic module resolution mode is unsupported.

questions.question: A service uses moduleResolution: node (node10). What should a TypeScript 7 migration typically select for code executed directly in modern Node.js?
questions.answer: nodenext
questions.explanation: node/node10 resolution is no longer supported. nodenext matches modern Node semantics; bundler is generally appropriate for bundler-managed projects.

questions.question: What should a team do with a TypeScript 6 project that relies on compilerOptions.baseUrl when moving to TypeScript 7?
options: Keep baseUrl and suppress the error indefinitely.
Remove baseUrl and adjust paths mappings to be relative to the project root as appropriate.
Convert every TypeScript import to require without checking runtime behavior.
questions.answer: Remove baseUrl and adjust paths mappings to be relative to the project root as appropriate.
questions.explanation: baseUrl is no longer supported in 7.0. Paths entries should be updated as needed; runtime/bundler resolution must be aligned separately.

questions.question: What is the purpose of stable type ordering in TypeScript 7?
options: To guarantee alphabetical ordering of every union type
To support deterministic ordering despite parallel compilation, reducing order-dependent diagnostics and declaration differences
To sort object properties at JavaScript runtime
To replace union types with tuples
questions.answer: To support deterministic ordering despite parallel compilation, reducing order-dependent diagnostics and declaration differences
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 uses deterministic type/symbol ordering across workers. stableTypeOrdering is effectively always enabled in 7.0.

questions.question: Which TypeScript 6 compiler option helps expose ordering-sensitive differences before upgrading to TypeScript 7?
questions.answer: stableTypeOrdering
questions.explanation: Enabling --stableTypeOrdering in 6.0 approximates 7.0 ordering; it can be slower and is a migration diagnostic rather than a permanent performance recommendation.

questions.question: Why might TypeScript-aware tools built on the TypeScript compiler API need special handling with TypeScript 7.0?
options: TypeScript 7.0 does not ship a public programmatic compiler API; a compatibility TypeScript 6 package can be used where needed.
TypeScript 7 makes type annotations execute in production.
TypeScript 7 rejects JSX syntax in all files.
questions.answer: TypeScript 7.0 does not ship a public programmatic compiler API; a compatibility TypeScript 6 package can be used where needed.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7.0 focuses on compiler and language-server functionality. The team provided @typescript/typescript6 for tools that still require the old programmatic API.

questions.question: What protocol underpins TypeScript 7.0 editor integration?
questions.answer: Language Server Protocol (LSP)
questions.explanation: The new language service supports LSP, allowing editors to use a faster, multithreaded server.

questions.question: TypeScript 7 changes template literal type inference. What is HeadTail<"😀abc"> for type HeadTail<S> = S extends `${infer Head}${infer Tail}` ? [Head, Tail] : never?
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 splits Unicode code points instead of separating UTF-16 surrogate halves when inferring template literal segments.

questions.question: Which JSON import attribute syntax should be used with TypeScript 7?
questions.answer: import data from "./a.json" with { type: "json" };
questions.explanation: The old asserts form was deprecated during the transition; modern import attributes use with. Runtime and configuration support must still be considered.

questions.question: A JavaScript/JSDoc codebase is being checked with TypeScript 7. Which changes should reviewers anticipate?
options: Types may need explicit typeof value expressions when referencing runtime values from type positions.
Closure-style JSDoc function(string): void remains the preferred supported syntax.
Legacy special recognition of @enum is removed.
Every JSDoc type is now enforced at runtime by TypeScript.
answers: Types may need explicit typeof value expressions when referencing runtime values from type positions.
Legacy special recognition of @enum is removed.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 simplifies JSDoc analysis: values in type positions should use typeof, and @enum no longer has special recognition. This remains static analysis only.

questions.question: TypeScript 7 makes interface and type declarations available as runtime validators for incoming JSON.
questions.explanation: The Go rewrite changes compiler implementation and speed, not type erasure or runtime input validation.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes TypeScript 7 --watch mode?
options: It is a rebuilt file-watching implementation informed by the Parcel watcher, rather than relying purely on expensive polling.
It automatically deploys builds to a Kubernetes cluster.
It executes JavaScript microtasks in a different order.
questions.answer: It is a rebuilt file-watching implementation informed by the Parcel watcher, rather than relying purely on expensive polling.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 rebuilt watch mode using a Go port derived from the Parcel watcher for efficient cross-platform change detection.

questions.question: In TypeScript 7, if the current directory contains tsconfig.json, what is required to compile explicitly listed source filenames from the CLI instead of using that config?
questions.answer: Pass --ignoreConfig with those file paths.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7 requires --ignoreConfig for command-line source file arguments when tsconfig.json exists in the working directory.

questions.question: Which steps are sensible in a production migration from TypeScript 6 to 7?
options: Clear 6.0 deprecations rather than relying on ignoreDeprecations.
Benchmark type-check times, memory, and CI concurrency on representative projects.
Check dependencies on TypeScript compiler APIs and editor plugins.
Assume faster compilation removes any need for integration testing.
answers: Clear 6.0 deprecations rather than relying on ignoreDeprecations.
Benchmark type-check times, memory, and CI concurrency on representative projects.
Check dependencies on TypeScript compiler APIs and editor plugins.
questions.explanation: TS7 is a substantial tooling migration; resolve deprecated options, benchmark build resources, and audit tools that embed TS before adopting it broadly.

questions.question: A fire-and-forget call to sendEmail() returns a Promise that may reject. What should production code do?
options: Ignore it because promises never cause failures after return.
Attach an explicit rejection handler or arrange observed task supervision and error reporting.
Wrap only the call expression in a synchronous try/catch without awaiting.
Call Promise.resolve() and assume the error disappears.
questions.answer: Attach an explicit rejection handler or arrange observed task supervision and error reporting.
questions.explanation: Unobserved rejections can be lost or trigger runtime-specific unhandled rejection behavior. Own the task lifecycle and capture/report failures.

questions.question: Which statements about optional chaining are correct?
options: obj?.address?.city avoids accessing city when an earlier link is null or undefined.
obj?.fn() suppresses errors when obj.fn is a non-function string.
Optional chaining automatically catches network or Promise errors.
answers: obj?.address?.city avoids accessing city when an earlier link is null or undefined.
obj?.missing may evaluate to undefined.
questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits on nullish receivers, not arbitrary errors. Invoking an existing non-callable member still throws.

questions.question: What happens for const cfg = { port: 3000, typo: true } satisfies { port: number };?
options: It is accepted because satisfies skips all extra properties.
A fresh object literal triggers an excess-property error for typo.
questions.answer: A fresh object literal triggers an excess-property error for typo.
questions.explanation: satisfies checks the fresh literal against the target object shape, including excess-property checking.

questions.question: An application models dynamic API response values as Record<string, number>. What is an important safety concern?
options: It validates that every runtime entry is numeric.
It permits indexing arbitrary keys at the type level, but a missing key can still return undefined at runtime.
questions.answer: It permits indexing arbitrary keys at the type level, but a missing key can still return undefined at runtime.
questions.explanation: Record is only a static model. Consider runtime validation and noUncheckedIndexedAccess when indexing potentially absent keys.
